lesson.title: Gift, Rat & Co.
lesson.subtitle: The six highest-value false friends — contrastive recall drills

hook.title: The Six Most Dangerous Words
hook.content: The full trap deck waits in the Review Hub, but six traps deserve early warning. das Gift = POISON (present: das Geschenk — and Gift really is gift's twin: both meant 'a giving', German kept the dose). bekommen = GET (become = werden). der Chef = BOSS (cook = der Koch). der Rat = ADVICE (rodent = die Ratte). fast = ALMOST (quick = schnell). bald = SOON (hairless = kahl). Each one is a true cognate that drifted — which is why the traps feel so natural. Drill the antidotes until the trap fires the correction automatically.

footnotes.title: Rat and Read Are Twins
footnotes.content: der Rat (advice) and English 'read' are the same ancient verb — *rēdanō, 'to advise, to interpret'. A counselor was a reader of situations. So der Rat is not just a trap: it is a hidden cognate pair (Rat/read) wearing a false-friend costume (Rat/rat).

pattern.title: The Antidote Table
pattern.content: Poison → das Gift; present → das Geschenk. Get → bekommen; become → werden. Boss → der Chef; cook → der Koch. Advice → der Rat; rodent → die Ratte. Almost → fast; quick → schnell. Soon → bald; hairless → kahl. The memory trick is the drift story: Gift once meant any administered dose (a gift can kill); bekommen is 'come by' (packages come by); bald was 'boldly soon' (*balþaz, kin to bold). Know the story and the trap disarms itself.
pattern.linguist_note: False friends cluster in high-frequency function words precisely because those words had time to drift. The rare words stayed put. Guard the small words hardest.

exercises.prompt: 'Vorsicht, das ist Gift!' — what is the warning about?
exercises.explanation: Vorsicht (caution!) + Gift = the poison warning. The present is das Geschenk.

exercises.prompt: 'Der Chef sagt: bald!' — what did the boss communicate?
exercises.explanation: Two traps in one sentence: the boss (not cook) wants it soon (not hairless).

exercises.prompt: Match each trap with its true meaning — and its antidote:
exercises.target_answer: bekommen, der Rat, fast, der Chef, die Fabrik, das Gymnasium, die Rente, der Dom
exercises.meaning: get, advice, almost, boss, factory, grammar-school, pension, cathedral
exercises.explanation: Eight traps, each wearing an English look-alike. The first four come with antidotes: bekommen is get (werden is become), der Rat is advice (die Ratte is the rodent), fast is almost (schnell is quick), der Chef is boss (der Koch is the cook). The last four have look-alikes too — fabric, gym, rent, dome — but die Fabrik is a factory, das Gymnasium a grammar school, die Rente a pension and der Dom a cathedral.

exercises.prompt: Which everyday English verb is the HIDDEN twin of 'der Rat' (via *rēdanō, to advise)?
exercises.explanation: The counselor read the situation: Rat and read are one verb. The trap is a cognate in disguise. And eventuell means possibly, not eventually — that one is schließlich.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the safe sentence: 'I am getting advice from the boss'
exercises.meaning: I am getting advice from the boss

vocab_hints.note: vom = von + dem — the dative contraction
the honorific that fronts a surname — Herr Chef, or Herr Braun when no job title fits
die Art = KIND, not art — art is die Kunst

exercises.explanation: All three traps used CORRECTLY: bekomme (get), Rat (advice), Chef (boss) — the minefield, disarmed. The hints carry two more small ones: die Art is the kind (art is die Kunst), and Herr is the Mister in front of a surname.

summary.outcome: Recall the six highest-value traps and their antidotes on sight.

use_example.english: I am getting advice from the boss.

summary.takeaway: Gift=poison (Geschenk=present), bekommen=get, Chef=boss, Rat=advice, fast=almost, bald=soon — drill the antidotes.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: ü, ö, ä — the three mouth positions English never taught you.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Gift, Rat & Co. (I am getting advice from the boss):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich bekomme Rat vom Chef" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Gift, Rat & Co. without relying on short-term echo.

gift.context_translation: The poison is in the glass!
gift.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *giftiz 'a giving/dose' — the true twin of gift; German kept the deadly-dose branch. Trap: das Gift = POISON. (Present: das Geschenk.) [wiktionary]

bekommen.etymology_derivation: be- (by/around) + kommen (come) — literally 'come by (something)'; English become is the same be + come with a different job. [wiktionary]

chef.context_translation: The boss is in the office.
chef.etymology_derivation: The true twin of chief (both from Latin caput via French) — but German kept the workplace sense. Trap: der Chef = BOSS. (Cook: der Koch.) [wiktionary]

rat.etymology_derivation: Ancient Germanic 'counsel' — the same root as 'read' (rædan, to advise!). Trap: der Rat = ADVICE. (Rodent: die Ratte.) [wiktionary]

fast.etymology_derivation: Ancient Germanic 'firmly, almost' — true cognate of fast in its 'firm' sense. Trap: fast = ALMOST. (Quick: schnell.) [wiktionary]

bald.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *balþaz — kin to English bold; the 'daring' became 'soon'. Trap: bald = SOON. (Hairless: kahl.) [wiktionary]

herr.context_translation: The gentleman is called Mr. Müller.
herr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hairaz 'grey' — the grey-haired one, cognate with English hoar. [wiktionary]

fabrik.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin fabrica — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Fabrik = FACTORY. (Fabric: der Stoff.) [wiktionary]

gymnasium.etymology_derivation: Both from the Greek wrestling-ground — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: das Gymnasium = ACADEMIC HIGH SCHOOL. (Gym: die Turnhalle.) [wiktionary]

rente.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin rendere — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Rente = PENSION. (Apartment rent: die Miete.) [wiktionary]

dom.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin domus (church-house) — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: der Dom = CATHEDRAL. (Dome: die Kuppel.) [wiktionary]

art.context_phrase: Diese Art von Buch ist gut.
art.context_translation: This kind of book is good.
art.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin ars/artis — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Art = KIND/TYPE. (Fine art: die Kunst.) [wiktionary]

kaution.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin cautio — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Kaution = SECURITY DEPOSIT. (Caution: die Vorsicht.) [wiktionary]

eventuell.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin eventus — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: eventuell = POSSIBLY. (Eventually: schließlich/am Ende.) [wiktionary]

patient.context_translation: The patient waits in the waiting room.
patient.etymology_derivation: From Latin patiens, the present participle of pati, to suffer — the same participle that gave English patient through Old French; a weak noun with plural Patienten. [wiktionary][etymonline]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
